working_title: Electric vs Push Golf Trolley: How to Actually Choose for UK Walking Golfers
angle: Most trolley guides either push you straight to electric or stay mealy-mouthed about the trade-offs. This post cuts through it for the regular UK walker: hilly or flat course, boot space, playing frequency, and budget are the real deciding factors, not which looks flashier in a showroom. The tone is practical and direct, with a clear framework for making the decision rather than a vague 'it depends'.
research_notes:
- Two dominant UK electric trolley brands: PowaKaddy (founded 1983, based in Sittingbourne, Kent; FX and CT ranges current) and Motocaddy — both named repeatedly across UK buyer guides as market leaders
- Electric trolleys in UK market range roughly from ~£499 (e.g. Motocaddy SE, described as best value entry-level electric) up to £1,249 (e.g. PowaKaddy CT12 GPS) in 2026 — these are retailer-listed prices from The Golf Shop Online, usable as general price-range framing but do not present them as definitive RRPs
- Push trolleys considerably cheaper: PowaKaddy Micra listed at £189, Clicgear 4.0 at £219 (The Golf Shop Online, 2026)
- Motocaddy Cube described as a compact push option, praised for folding small and being lightweight — approximate price around £150
- Key electric trolley buying factors for UK context: battery size (18-hole vs 27/36-hole lithium — match to course length and hilliness); folded size vs car boot; electronic braking systems (EBS) flagged as important for steep UK courses; motor/voltage specs vary by model
- Electric trolleys heavier and bulkier due to motor and battery; push trolleys lighter, easier to store, more storage compartments as standard
- Remote-control electric trolleys a growing segment: Motocaddy ME Remote (2026) described as best entry-level remote option; Motocaddy M7 GPS Remote and PowaKaddy RX12 GPS at higher end
- Follow (auto-follow) trolleys exist (e.g. Stewart Q Follow) but at a significantly higher price point — niche segment, relevant to mention briefly
- Push trolleys noted to generally offer more integrated storage than electric models
- EBS (electronic braking system) a practical feature for hilly UK parkland and links courses
- Lithium vs lead-acid battery: lithium now standard on modern UK electric trolleys — lighter, faster to charge, longer lifespan
- For context: UK golfers typically walk rather than ride carts, making trolley choice a more significant decision than in cart-dominant markets like the US
- Key decision framework: course terrain (hilly = stronger case for electric), playing frequency, car boot dimensions, and total budget
- Trolley warranties typically split: separate warranty for frame and battery on electric models
must_avoid:
- Do not fabricate specific prices beyond those noted above from retailer sources; describe ranges in general terms if uncertain
- Do not invent specs (motor wattage, weight figures) beyond what is in research notes
- Do not quote or attribute any real reviewer quotes — none were gathered for this brief
- No health/injury advice beyond the well-known general point that walking with a trolley reduces fatigue vs carrying (do not make specific medical claims about joints, back conditions, etc.)
- No affiliate links unless the product is on the approved-partners list — mention brands and models informationally only if not approved; do not flag this to the reader in the post body
- No em dashes anywhere in the post or title
- No invented personal anecdotes about playing specific courses with specific trolleys
- This is not a 'best of' product roundup post: it is a decision-framework/how-to-choose guide, consistent with the site's existing Gear tone (cf. stand-bag, waterproof jacket, mid-layer posts) — keep it practical and avoid turning it into a thinly veiled product listicle
